title: Concurrent Audit | Audit Services
headings: Think of it as an early-warning system
When Is It Useful For a Business?
summary: Near-real-time examination of transactions, controls and compliance so significant exceptions can be identified while operations are still continuing.
Live / near-real-time audit support for financial entities
Designed around the institution's approved audit scope, applicable RBI instructions, internal policies, risk profile and engagement terms.

Concurrent audit is an examination performed contemporaneously with transactions, or as near to the transaction as possible. RBI describes it as an important early-warning mechanism for timely detection of irregularities and lapses.
Early detection: Exceptions can be identified before they become larger control, operational or financial problems.
Stronger controls: Transactions can be checked against approved policies, delegated authority and applicable instructions.

sections.heading: What Is Concurrent Audit? / How it helps an organisation
sections.text: What Is Concurrent Audit? / How it helps an organisation — Concurrent audit is an examination performed contemporaneously with transactions, or as near to the transaction as possible. RBI describes it as an important early-warning mechanism for timely detection of irregularities and lapses. Early detection: Exceptions can be identified before they become larger control, operational or financial problems. Stronger controls: Transactions can be checked against approved policies, delegated authority and applicable instructions. Fraud-risk reduction: RBI's framework specifically highlights fraud-prone areas such as cash, deposits, advances, forex, off-balance-sheet items, cards and internet banking. Faster escalation: Serious irregularities can be reported promptly to the appropriate management level for action. Management assurance: Findings provide management and the Audit Committee…

sections.heading: Who Benefits From Concurrent Audit? / Banks & Financial Institutions
sections.text: Who Benefits From Concurrent Audit? / Banks & Financial Institutions — Concurrent audit is primarily relevant to regulated or high-risk financial operations rather than ordinary personal finances. Particularly useful for high-risk branches, specialised branches, centralised processing units and activities such as treasury, forex, retail assets, corporate/SME operations and other areas identified for concurrent review. Audit design should be aligned with the entity's applicable RBI framework, risk profile and internal audit architecture. RBI's RBIA framework applies to specified NBFC categories and focuses on governance, risk management and controls. Generally not a personal compliance requirement. An individual normally needs tax, accounting or financial-planning services instead. Concurrent audit becomes relevant only where the person operates or controls an organisation whose…

sections.heading: When Is It Useful For a Business? / Situations where it adds value
sections.text: When Is It Useful For a Business? / Situations where it adds value — The strongest business case exists where transaction volume, regulatory exposure, operational complexity or fraud risk makes retrospective checking too slow. Large transaction volumes or multiple operational locations. High-risk branches, departments or products. Loan processing, cash operations, deposits and other sensitive financial activities. Centralised processing units where large-scale operations create concentrated risk. Operations requiring prompt exception reporting and rectification. It is not a replacement for every other audit. Statutory audit, internal audit, risk-based internal audit, compliance reviews and other assurance functions can have different objectives and scopes. It is also not a guarantee that fraud or error can never occur. Its value is in improving the probability of timely…

sections.heading: Is Concurrent Audit Useful For You Personally? / You may need other services
sections.text: Is Concurrent Audit Useful For You Personally? / You may need other services — For a salaried person, freelancer, small individual investor or ordinary household, concurrent audit is generally not the appropriate service. Tax planning and compliance Personal financial documentation Investment or loan documentation support Ordinary household expenses Personal tax filing by itself

sections.heading: What Can Happen If You Do Not Do It? / Delayed Detection
sections.text: What Can Happen If You Do Not Do It? / Delayed Detection — The consequence depends on whether concurrent audit is required by regulation, the institution's approved policy, or the engagement framework. It is not correct to say that every business automatically faces a statutory penalty simply for not having a concurrent audit. Control failures, unusual transactions or documentation gaps may remain unnoticed for longer, increasing the cost and difficulty of correction. Where high-risk transactions are not independently reviewed promptly, opportunities for irregularities or fraudulent manipulation may be harder to detect early. If an applicable regulatory requirement or approved institutional policy requires concurrent audit, failure to implement or properly follow it can create compliance and governance concerns and may lead to adverse audit observations or escalation.

sections.heading: What Can Be Checked? / Cash & Banking
sections.text: What Can Be Checked? / Cash & Banking — The exact checklist is determined by the appointing institution and its approved audit scope. RBI's commercial-bank framework provides examples of key areas. Cash transactions, cash verification, remittances and related controls. Loan documentation and transaction checks where included in scope. Deposit-related transactions, controls and compliance checks. Specialised financial activities where applicable. Credit-card and internet-banking related risk areas where covered. Checks against applicable internal procedures, delegated authority and regulatory instructions.

sections.heading: Concurrent Audit Process / Define Scope
sections.text: Concurrent Audit Process / Define Scope — A practical engagement normally moves from scope definition to review, exception reporting, rectification and follow-up. Identify locations, products, risk areas, records and applicable instructions. Examine transactions as they occur or as close to occurrence as practicable. Document deviations, control gaps and unusual or high-risk observations. Minor issues may be corrected promptly; serious matters should be escalated according to the approved reporting system. Track management action and ensure important observations are closed or appropriately reported.

sections.heading: 2026 Information & Regulatory Reference
sections.text: 2026 Information & Regulatory Reference — This page is reviewed for 2026 using official RBI material. The principal commercial-bank concurrent-audit guideline located is RBI's July 16, 2015 revised guideline; RBI's 2021 RBIA framework is separately relevant to specified NBFCs and UCBs.

sections.text: Due Diligence — A structured review of financial, tax, legal, commercial and operational information before an investment, acquisition, lending decision, restructuring or other material transaction. sections.heading: Why It Matters Before a Transaction / How it can help a business
sections.text: Why It Matters Before a Transaction / How it can help a business — A disciplined review can turn scattered documents into a structured risk picture before money, ownership or contractual obligations change hands. Identify financial or operational issues before an investor or buyer discovers them. Prepare supporting records and explanations for lender, investor or acquirer review. Improve negotiation readiness by identifying liabilities, gaps and commercial dependencies. Prioritise corrective actions before closing or signing a major transaction. Create a documented risk trail for management and transaction advisers. Routine low-value purchases or ordinary operating decisions. Transactions where there is no meaningful financial, ownership or contractual exposure. Situations where the proposed scope duplicates a specialist review that already addresses the relevant risk. It should not…

sections.heading: What Can Happen If You Skip It? / Potential consequences for a business
sections.text: What Can Happen If You Skip It? / Potential consequences for a business — Skipping due diligence does not automatically make a transaction wrong, but it can reduce the information available before the decision becomes difficult or expensive to reverse. Unexpected liabilities, debt or working-capital pressure may emerge after the transaction. Tax, statutory or contractual issues may require additional remediation or negotiation. Weak records can reduce confidence during investor, lender or acquirer review. Overstated revenue, margins or business assumptions may affect valuation and deal economics. Post-transaction disputes can become harder to manage when facts were not documented before closing. SEBI's investor guidance recommends checking fundamentals and the risk-return profile before investing. Due diligence should therefore be viewed as an information and risk-assessment…

sections.heading: How the Review Works / Typical workflow
sections.text: How the Review Works / Typical workflow — The exact workflow is tailored to the engagement, but a practical review normally follows these stages. Define scope: transaction purpose, entities, period, materiality and required specialists. Collect records: financial, tax, statutory, contractual and operational information. Validate: compare records, explanations and available supporting evidence. Assess risks: identify gaps, unusual items, liabilities and dependencies. Report: present observations, priority issues and recommended next actions. Financial statements, ledgers, bank information and management accounts. Tax returns, notices and material statutory records. Loan agreements, security details and material commitments. Major customer/vendor contracts and related-party information. Corporate, ownership and other transaction-specific documents.

sections.heading: Regulatory & Professional Context
sections.text: Regulatory & Professional Context — These references provide context for due diligence. The applicable requirement depends on the entity, transaction and governing framework. SEBI Investor: Due diligence before investing includes understanding the business, business model, financial health and other material investment information. Official SEBI guidance → SEBI AIF framework: SEBI has prescribed specific due-diligence requirements relating to investors and investments of AIFs. Official SEBI circular → ICAI: ICAI's professional learning material includes Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Audit as a dedicated area of auditing and assurance. Official ICAI source → 2026 banking context: ICAI released its Guidance Note on Audit of Banks (2026 Edition) on 16 March 2026. Official ICAI 2026 source →

sections.heading: Before You Commit / Good due diligence asks
sections.text: Before You Commit / Good due diligence asks — For a significant transaction, ask whether you have enough verified information to understand the downside—not only the expected upside. What are we buying? What obligations come with it? Are the financial numbers supportable? What compliance or tax exposures exist? Which assumptions are still unverified? What should be resolved before signing? A due-diligence report is based on the agreed scope, records made available, procedures performed and applicable professional requirements. It cannot provide absolute assurance that every fraud, error, liability or future event will be identified.

sections.heading: How Forensic Audit Is Useful / Useful For Businesses
sections.text: How Forensic Audit Is Useful / Useful For Businesses — A forensic audit is most useful when there is a specific risk, allegation, unusual transaction pattern, financial dispute or suspected misuse of funds that requires evidence-based examination. Fraud investigation: helps examine suspected misappropriation, diversion of funds, manipulation of records or unusual transactions. Management decisions: provides a structured fact base when management needs to decide what happened and what corrective action may be required. Lenders and investors: can help investigate concerns about financial statements, fund utilisation or transaction trails before or after a material exposure. Dispute support: can organise financial evidence and transaction trails for review by the appropriate legal or regulatory professionals. Root-cause analysis: can identify control weaknesses that allowed an…

sections.heading: Who Does Not Normally Need a Forensic Audit? / Usually Not Necessary For
sections.text: Who Does Not Normally Need a Forensic Audit? / Usually Not Necessary For — Forensic audit is investigation-oriented. It should not be presented as a compulsory service for every business or individual. Routine bookkeeping, accounting or GST/Income-tax compliance where there is no investigation issue. Ordinary annual financial reporting where the objective is a statutory or financial-statement audit. Normal personal banking, salary income and everyday household finances. Minor discrepancies that can be resolved through normal reconciliation and internal controls. If the requirement is routine compliance, bookkeeping, tax filing or ordinary financial-statement assurance, another service may be more appropriate. If the question is “What actually happened, where did the money go, who was involved, and what evidence supports the conclusion?” , a forensic approach may be appropriate.

sections.heading: What If You Do Not Investigate a Suspected Irregularity? / Possible Business Consequences
sections.text: What If You Do Not Investigate a Suspected Irregularity? / Possible Business Consequences — Not every suspected irregularity requires a forensic audit. However, ignoring a material warning sign can allow the underlying issue to continue or make evidence harder to reconstruct later. Continuing financial leakage: an unresolved diversion or control weakness may continue to create losses. Evidence deterioration: transaction records, emails, approvals and other supporting evidence may become harder to obtain or correlate over time. Regulatory escalation: for regulated entities, fraud-risk frameworks can require timely detection, reporting and follow-up of fraud incidents. Reputational damage: unresolved material financial irregularities can affect lenders, investors, customers and other stakeholders. Legal and recovery difficulty: weak documentation or delayed investigation can make…

sections.heading: When Should You Consider It? / Business Warning Signs
sections.text: When Should You Consider It? / Business Warning Signs — The trigger is normally a defined risk or question that ordinary reconciliation or routine audit procedures cannot adequately resolve. Unexplained cash withdrawals or transfers. Repeated transactions with related parties or connected entities that require examination. Revenue, expense or asset balances that do not reconcile with supporting evidence. Suspected diversion or misuse of borrowed or company funds. Complaints from lenders, investors, shareholders or management about financial irregularities. Unusual patterns identified through internal audit, data analysis or whistle-blower information. Possible examples include a serious partnership or family-business financial dispute, suspected misuse of jointly controlled business funds, unexplained movement of material assets, or a financial matter where transaction reconstruction…

sections.heading: Current Regulatory & Professional Context / Official References
sections.text: Current Regulatory & Professional Context / Official References — There is no single rule saying that every Indian business or individual must obtain a forensic audit. The requirement and scope depend on the entity, circumstances, applicable regulation and engagement purpose. RBI — Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2024: applicable regulated entities have frameworks for prevention, early detection and timely reporting of fraud. The Directions also contain provisions on the role of auditors and independent confirmation from third-party professionals. RBI official source → RBI — NBFC Fraud Risk Management Directions, 2024: applicable NBFCs are subject to a framework for prevention, early detection and timely reporting of fraud.
